transcript:
>> This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Hurst.
With months to go to the midterm elections and control of Congress at stake,
the economy is high on voters' minds.
This is the labor market wobbled a bit last month
as employers only added 29,000 jobs, well below forecasts
of around 84,000 jobs expected to be created
and sending the unemployment rate slightly higher to 4.2%.
For black people, the unemployment rate is growing
up to a full percentage point to 7% month over month according
to the Labor Department's monthly jobs report.
White House economic advisor Kevin Hassett.
>> It's definitely a cause for concern and it's something
that we're studying very closely.
>> The unemployment rate for all other races tracked
by the federal government, Asian, Hispanic,
and white fell during that time.
With just weeks to go to the elections,
President Trump is now on a campaign rally swing including
in traditional Republican stronghold states.
Today stopping in Ohio yesterday, he was in Alabama.
And the Republican controlled Georgia election board has asked the
Justice Department to investigate and intervene
in the state's election system with voting set
to begin October 13th.
And Pierce Frank Langford has more.
>> In the letter earlier this week,
Georgia election board head James Mills said the state system is
easily compromised and urged the Justice Department
to pressure the Georgia Secretary of State
to oversee installation of a software patch
to eliminate security vulnerabilities.
He also urged the DOJ to prohibit use
of certain voting machines.
The Secretary of State's office dismissed the demand.
Quote, "People who are serious
about election security don't inject chaos in the 11th hour,"
a spokesperson told Georgia Public Broadcasting.
The call for federal intervention comes
as polls show Georgia Democratic Senator John Ossoff well ahead
of his opponent, Republican Representative Mike Collins.
Frank Langford, NPR News.
>> Cornell University says an outside counsel will investigate
the school's handling of a sex assault allegation
against seven students in 2024.
New York's Governor Kathy Hochul had been calling
for an independent investigation.
A county prosecutor reopened its investigation
after the woman making the accusations filed a civil lawsuit.
>> It appears Jacqueline Diaz has more.
>> Trauma has a way of affecting someone's brain,
behavior, and memory.
There may be gaps in holes
in an assault survivor's story to police.
That may be due in part to how officers question them.
Dave Thompson is a certified forensic interviewer
and a consultant who trains investigators
and interrogation techniques.
>> Our memories don't work like a video recorder
that we can just rewind, hit play,
and remember from start to finish what happened.
>> Dave Thompson says investigators handling these
cases should be trained in trauma-informed policing
so they can use that knowledge to help build trust,
which has a big effect on an investigation.
Jacqueline Diaz, NPR News.
>> You're listening to NPR News.
In Spain, protests are taking place across the country a week
after thousands took to the streets to demand urgent action
by the government to address a national housing crisis.
It all started with the eviction of an 87-year-old woman,
but as NPR's Miguel Macias reports, that was just the spark.
>> Much has happened since the protests started a week ago
after 87-year-old Maria del Carmen Abascal was evicted
from her rental apartment in Madrid.
The government of Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez drafted two
emergency housing decrees in a rush negotiating
with these coalition members.
While all parties in Spain agree there's a national problem,
with the price of rental housing,
they did not agree on a solution.
On Friday, Sanchez's measures were voted down.
In Congress, there's been plenty of finger-pointing
and speculation that Sanchez might call snap elections
for late November as he sees an opportunity to come
from behind in the polls thanks to an energized left.
On the streets, protesters continue
to demand solutions now.
Miguel Macias, NPR News, Seville, Spain.
>> Experts of Southern California are under dangerous,
long-lasting heat wave,
and the National Weather Service has issued heat warnings
for several areas.
That also has officials warning about the increased risk
of fast-moving wildfires.
Southern California Edison says thousands of customers are
under consideration for power shutoffs to reduce the risk
of electrical equipment sparking a fire.
I'm Janine Herbst, NPR News in Washington.
>> Want to hear this podcast without sponsor breaks?
Amazon Prime members can listen to NPR News now,

Or you can also support NPR's vital journalism

That's plus.npr.org.

topics.text: U.S. employers added only 29,000 jobs last month, unemployment rate rises to 4.2%
Black unemployment rate increases one percentage point to 7% according to Labor Department
President Trump campaigns in Ohio and Alabama as midterm elections approach
Georgia election board requests Justice Department investigate state election system vulnerabilities
Cornell University to hire outside counsel to investigate handling of 2024 sex assault case
Trauma-informed policing training helps investigators build trust with sexual assault survivors
Thousands protest across Spain demanding government action on national housing crisis
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's emergency housing measures voted down in Congress
Southern California under dangerous heat wave with increased wildfire risk warnings
